headline: Your MVP doesn't need perfect architecture. It needs decisions you can undo.

slides.html:
Your MVP doesn’t need perfect architecture.

It needs decisions you can undo.

How to tell which early choices deserve a week of thought — and which deserve an hour.

Two ways MVPs go wrong

Teams treat every decision the same.

Some debate everything. Three weeks choosing a CI tool, a queue, a framework — before a single user has signed up.

Some debate nothing. The data model and the public API get decided in a hurry, then customers build on top of them.

One-way doors and two-way doors

In Amazon’s 2015 shareholder letter, Jeff Bezos separated decisions into two types.

One-way door — hard or impossible to reverse. Slow down, think it through.

Two-way door — if it’s wrong, you walk back through. Decide fast, with a small group.
Sort by the cost to undo

Same sprint. Two decisions.

Background job library

Nothing outside the codebase sees it. Swapping it later is a few days of work. Pick one this afternoon.

Webhook payload format

The day a customer integrates, it becomes their code too. Version it from day one and review it properly.

Three questions before you decide

01

Who builds on it? If customers, partners or stored data depend on it, treat it as one-way.

02

What would undoing cost? Estimate it in weeks, not feelings.

03

Can we add a seam? An interface or adapter can turn a one-way door into a two-way one.

Remember this

Speed in an MVP comes from deciding reversible things quickly — not from deciding everything quickly.

Spend your design time where customers and data will lock you in.

Write down which doors you treated as one-way, and why.

Which early decision turned out to be a one-way door?

The one you wish you had spent another week on.
